title: 2 Timothy
subtitle: A prisoner's last letter to his son in the faith
lead: 2 Timothy is written as Paul's last letter. He is in chains in Rome, he has already faced a first hearing in court, and he expects to die soon: "I am already a drink offering being poured out" (4:6). He writes to Timothy, his closest coworker and his "child", to call him to Rome before winter and to hand on to him the work he is leaving: do not be ashamed, suffer for the good news, guard the teaching, entrust it to faithful people, proclaim the word. The letter is warm and personal, full of names and memories, tears and longing, desertions and loyal friends.

It is also the source of some of the most quoted lines in the New Testament: "God did not give us a spirit of cowardice" (1:7), "Every Scripture is God-breathed" (3:16), and "I have competed in the good contest. I have run the course to the finish. I have kept the faith" (4:7). It is one of the three Pastoral Letters, with 1 Timothy and Titus, and whether Paul wrote them is one of the great questions of New Testament study. This page and the topic "The Pastoral Letters" present the views fairly. The Plain follows the letter as written and says "Paul" where it does.
facts: Traditionally Paul (1:1), writing from prison in Rome (1:8, 17). Many critical scholars hold that a follower wrote all three Pastoral Letters after Paul's death; some think 2 Timothy contains real notes from Paul, and some think 2 Timothy, the most likely of the three to be Paul's, has a different author from 1 Timothy and Titus. See "Who wrote it" below and the topic "The Pastoral Letters".
If Paul wrote it, near the end of his life, in a Roman imprisonment under Nero, in the 60s AD. If a follower wrote it, some decades later, often placed between about AD 90 and 140.
Timothy, probably at Ephesus (1:18; 4:12, 19), and the church with him (the last words, "Grace be with you", 4:22, use the plural "you").
A personal letter in the form of a farewell testament: a dying leader's charge to his successor.
Greek. Codex Vaticanus, one of the oldest nearly complete Greek Bibles, does not contain the Pastoral Letters; Codex Sinaiticus (300s) does.
authorship: The letter names Paul (1:1), speaks of his chains and his trial in Rome (1:8, 16-17; 4:16), of his coming death (4:6-8), and of friends and places known from Acts and Paul's other letters: Luke, Mark, Demas, Tychicus, Prisca and Aquila, Erastus, Trophimus, Troas, Miletus, Corinth.

From the second century the church read the letter as Paul's last. Eusebius (Church History 2.22), in the early 300s, passes on what "is said": that Paul was released after the two years of Acts 28 and sent out to preach again, and that he died on a second stay in Rome; he reads this letter as written in that second imprisonment, and in 2.25 he records that Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero. F. F. Bruce points out that even Eusebius introduces the release with "the story goes". 1 Clement (about AD 96) says Paul reached "the extreme limit of the west" before he died (chapter 5). J. N. D. Kelly's commentary (1963), as Bruce summarizes it, argued for the release and a second Roman imprisonment, and placed 4:9-18 between two hearings of Paul's case.

A number of scholars still defend Paul's authorship of 2 Timothy. Luke Timothy Johnson's Anchor Bible commentary (2001) makes what Craig Blomberg's review calls a "robust defense of Pauline authorship" of both letters to Timothy, and N. T. Wright (Paul: A Biography, 2018) is also named among the defenders. They stress the letter's personal details, the request for a cloak and books, the restored friendship with Mark, and the honest record of desertions. F. F. Bruce wrote that the "circumstantiality and incidental character" of the mention of Onesiphorus in Rome (1:16-18) "bespeak a genuine Pauline reminiscence", and he related it and the farewell of 4:6-18 to a late phase of Paul's Roman imprisonment.

Some explain the differences of style by a secretary who was given unusual freedom. C. F. D. Moule ("The Problem of the Pastoral Epistles: A Reappraisal", a lecture given in 1964), as F. F. Bruce reports, suggested that for these letters Paul used as his secretary a man he could trust with far more freedom than an ordinary secretary: Luke, the one companion still with him (4:11). The parts that do not sound like Paul would then reflect Luke's thought rather than Paul's. Bruce himself thought Luke might have served Paul in this way, or else collected and published what remained of Paul's letters after his death.

Since the 1800s many critical scholars have held that all three Pastoral Letters were written in Paul's name after his death, often dated between about AD 90 and 140. Their general reasons (vocabulary and style, church order, "faith" as a body of teaching, the opponents, travels that do not fit Acts) are set out on the topic "The Pastoral Letters" and are not repeated here. For 2 Timothy in particular they note that the travel details (Trophimus left at Miletus, 4:20; the cloak at Troas, 4:13) do not fit the journeys in Acts, and that the letter's form, a farewell testament, was a common way to write in the name of a great figure. Raymond E. Brown proposed that the writer was a follower of Paul who had knowledge of Paul's last days. Scholars on both sides of the question read the letter as a testament or farewell.
Real notes inside a later letter

P. N. Harrison (The Problem of the Pastoral Epistles, 1921) argued that the author was "a devout, sincere, and earnest Paulinist, who lived at Rome or Ephesus", writing "during the later years of Trajan or (? and) the earlier years of Hadrian's reign", but that he "had access to several brief personal notes written by the Apostle". In 2 Timothy, Harrison held, such notes were "added as a sort of appendix or postscript"; one was appended to Titus, and 1 Timothy has none. Bruce calls this the "fragment" hypothesis.

2 Timothy is sometimes said to be the most likely of the three to have been written by Paul, and some scholars conclude that its author was a different person from the author of 1 Timothy and Titus. Jerome Murphy-O'Connor was among those who defended the authenticity of 2 Timothy (Paul: A Critical Life).

The letter reads the same in either case as a call to faithfulness under pressure. What changes is the setting: Paul's own last weeks, or the next generation remembering him and handing on his authority. The notes say where a reading depends on the answer.

audience.to: Timothy, Paul's coworker since his second journey (Acts 16:1-3): a young man from Lystra, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, raised in the Jewish Scriptures by his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois (1:5; 3:15). He seems to be at or near Ephesus (1:18; 4:12, 19), in the province of Asia, where many have turned away from Paul (1:15) and where teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus are spreading a teaching that the resurrection is already past (2:17-18). Behind Timothy stands the church he leads: the letter ends "Grace be with you" (4:22) with a plural "you", so it was meant to be read aloud to them.
audience.why: Paul is in prison in Rome and expects to die. He writes to call Timothy to come before winter (4:9, 21) and to hand over his work: to keep the teaching (1:13-14), to entrust it to faithful people (2:2), to endure suffering (2:3), to correct opponents gently (2:24-26), to hold to the Scriptures (3:14-17), and to proclaim the word in all seasons (4:2). Knowing the audience changes the reading: the letter is not a general essay on church life but a charge to one leader at a dangerous time, whose teacher is in chains and whose friends are leaving. Its famous statements (on Scripture, on suffering, on finishing well) were first given to strengthen him.
views: The letter was sent to Timothy at Ephesus, as the mentions of Onesiphorus, Prisca and Aquila and Tychicus suggest.
Timothy was somewhere in the province of Asia; Tychicus' being sent to Ephesus (4:12) may mean that Timothy was not there.
The churches of a later generation
If a follower wrote it, the real readers were the churches of the late first or early second century, who heard Paul's last charge as addressed to their own leaders.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads 2 Timothy against a Roman prison, Nero's Rome, the province of Asia and Paul's network of coworkers; asks what a first defense, a chain, a cloak and a winter voyage meant, and what Eusebius and 1 Clement say of Paul's end.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the letter and when: Paul in his last imprisonment, a follower writing a testament in his name, or a later letter with genuine notes of Paul inside (Harrison). Weighs the travel details, the farewell form and the textual evidence.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a farewell testament: the charge to a successor, the images of soldier, athlete, farmer, vessel and drink offering, the trustworthy saying of 2:11-13, the vice list of 3:2-5, and the two loves of chapter 4.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's Jewish roots: Timothy's Jewish mother and grandmother, "the holy writings" learned in childhood, the Greek of Numbers 16:5 and Psalm 22:21, Jannes and Jambres in the Damascus Document, the Targum and the Talmud, the drink offering of the Law, and the farewell speeches of Moses and David.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads how the churches have used the letter: ordination and apostolic succession (1:6; 2:2), prayer for the dead (1:16-18), perseverance (2:12-13), the inspiration and authority of Scripture (3:16), and Linus and the bishops of Rome (4:21).

sections.b:
Read it as a letter from a man who expects to die, to a younger man he loves. The feeling is strong: tears and longing (1:4), shame and courage (1:8, 12, 16), loneliness (4:10-11, 16), gratitude (1:16-18), forgiveness (4:16) and hope (4:8, 18). The commands are simple and repeated: do not be ashamed, suffer with me, guard the deposit, entrust it to others, remember Jesus Christ, flee and pursue, remain in what you learned, proclaim the word, come quickly.

Key words keep the same English through the letter: deposit (what is entrusted), sound (healthy) teaching, godliness, appearing (Christ's coming into view), that day, and the verb suffer hard things.

1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus share a vocabulary and a concern for sound teaching and church leaders, and they are usually studied together (see "The Pastoral Letters"). 2 Timothy stands apart in three ways. It is the most personal, with more than twenty names. It says almost nothing about church offices: there are no lists for overseers or deacons. And its main theme is suffering and faithfulness to the end, in the face of death, rather than the ordering of a church.

Acts ends with Paul two years under guard in Rome, preaching "with complete freedom to speak, and no one stopped him" (Acts 28:31). It does not tell how he died. 1 Clement, written from Rome about AD 96, says that Paul was thrown into captivity seven times, preached in the east and the west, reached the extreme limit of the west and "bore testimony before the rulers" before he died (1 Clement 5, in F. F. Bruce's translation). Eusebius (Church History 2.22 and 2.25) passes on what "is said": that he was released, preached again, and died on a second stay in Rome; he places this letter there, and he records that Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero. The Roman historian Tacitus describes Nero's cruel punishment of the Christians after the great fire of Rome in AD 64 (Annals 15.44). 2 Timothy is read by many as the record of that last imprisonment, and by others as the next generation's portrait of it.

The Greek text of 2 Timothy is well preserved. Codex Vaticanus, a fourth-century Greek Bible, does not contain the Pastoral Letters; Codex Sinaiticus does, and Tischendorf's edition of it was checked for every variant on this site. The differences that change the English are small: "of the Gentiles" (1:11), "before the Lord" or "before God" (2:14), "the name of Christ" in the KJV (2:19), "at his appearing" (4:1), Galatia or Gaul (4:10), and whether 4:14 is a promise or a wish. The key clause of the famous verse on Scripture (3:16) has no variant; later in that verse the Byzantine text has another form of the word for "exposing". Each difference has its own entry. Small differences of spelling and word order that do not change the English are not entered.

spec.title: Claude's theory: shame and honor as the letter's spine
spec.body: The letter's appeals return again and again to shame. Timothy must not be ashamed of the testimony or of Paul (1:8); Paul is not ashamed (1:12); Onesiphorus was not ashamed of his chain (1:16); the approved worker has nothing to be ashamed of (2:15); vessels are for honor or dishonor (2:20-21). In a society where a prisoner's friends shared his disgrace, the letter may be built to turn the shame of chains into honor before God, ending with the crown (4:8) and the honor of being rescued and brought into the heavenly kingdom (4:18). Scholars have long studied honor and shame in the New Testament world; reading it as the organizing thread of this letter is my suggestion, and it rests on the repeated vocabulary rather than on any statement of the author's plan.

prompts: The prisoner writing his last letter

An old man in a dim Roman cell, sitting on straw with a chain at his ankle, writing on a sheet balanced on his knee by the light of a small clay lamp; a younger man, Luke, kneels nearby holding an ink pot; through a narrow high window the evening sky of Rome. Sketched onto a rolled parchment scroll in the style of an ancient manuscript drawing mixed with cave-painting ochre figures and loose modern watercolor washes; soft torn edges, no hard frame.

A runner's feet crossing a finish line drawn in the sand of an ancient stadium, a laurel wreath hanging above in the air, a cup of wine being poured out beside it like a drink offering, and a small boat casting off its rope in the background. Hand-sketched on a scroll in charcoal and ochre, hieroglyph-like figures and modern ink lines; soft edges, no rectangle.
Lois, Eunice and the child Timothy

In a simple house in Lystra, a grandmother and a mother sit with a small boy between them, a scroll of the Scriptures open across their laps, their fingers tracing the Greek letters; a loom and a water jar behind them. Drawn on old parchment with cave-drawing simplicity and warm modern watercolor, the edges of the scene fading into the scroll.
reading: P. N. Harrison, The Problem of the Pastoral Epistles (1921)
The classic study arguing from vocabulary that a later Paulinist wrote the Pastorals, with genuine notes of Paul built into 2 Timothy.
Eusebius, Church History, book 2, chapters 22 and 25 (about AD 325)
The early church's account of Paul's release, second imprisonment and death under Nero, and of when 2 Timothy was written.
The earliest account of Paul's sufferings and death, from the church in Rome.
Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum (1965), chapter 3
The Catholic Church's teaching on the inspiration and truth of Scripture, quoting 2 Timothy 3:16-17.
The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978)
An evangelical statement of the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture, in articles of affirmation and denial.
